question: What of a delivery of objects out of JOC is the handing of its samples from the pipeline to the file, and what is that worth written without a vector for every row?
method: Timers around the stages of a delivery of objects, in a throwaway build, over one stream of each kind of JOC stream the corpus has. The samples of every element wait on a queue until every element has them; the rows were then taken off the queues one sample at a time into a vector made for every row, and the writers of the object formats pushed the bytes of every sample onto a vector one sample at a time. The rows are taken into one buffer now, the samples of an object go straight onto its queue, and the writers put their bytes into buffers that are given their size first. The binary of main and the binary of the change were measured on a delivery of objects from one stream of each kind, turn and turn about bound to the fast cores, and on every command of the comparison (`tools/bench.py --compare`). The writers were measured each way inside one binary, in kernels of a throwaway worktree that hold the two forms of each as the two sources have them. That no byte moved was looked for over the corpus (`tools/old_new.py --decode-all`). The streams are media and are not in the repository.

where_the_time_of_a_delivery_of_objects_.how: timers in a throwaway build, `decode --format damf`, the run of three whose pipeline took least; the timers cost time themselves, so the shares are what is meant

a_delivery_of_objects_from_one_stream_of.how: `decode --format damf`, the binary of main and the binary of the change turn and turn about, five runs each after one that is not counted, bound to the fast cores

the_writers_each_way_inside_one_binary.how: kernels of the benchmark in a throwaway worktree, a frame of 1 536 rows of sixteen elements of noise over the 24 bits, `tools/kernels.py --affinity FFFF --runs 5`: the least of the medians of five runs
the_writers_each_way_inside_one_binary.reading: the frame of DAMF rows has an allocation in it, which grew four times a frame on main and is kept with the change, and a kernel measures that of a heap that holds nothing else: its figure is not one of the command

writing_the_rows_of_a_frame_inside_a_del.how: the stage of the timers, which has the disk in it, over the frames of the stream
writing_the_rows_of_a_frame_inside_a_del.reading: what the writers gained cannot be told there from what the disk does

the_binary_of_the_change_against_the_bin.reading: the writers of the object formats serve the object deliveries of TrueHD streams as well, which is where the two slower rows are from. They are written to a disk, which was busy in this run: the spread of those rows is 9 and 10 per cent, and the object formats of the run go from 0.72 to 1.38 of what they were. Measured again bound to the fast cores, nine runs each, they take a little less time than they did

what_the_first_run_found.reading: three things of the pipeline that were there before this change and that no test held: the fixture has a clip gain of one and a silent LFE, and the two object formats were held to each other, which they are when an object is in the wrong element of both. A test puts a pipeline through frames of the fixture with a payload that says another clip gain and a ramp for an LFE, and another holds the element of every object. All three are caught now

result.what_was_seen_and_left: When the stream ends, the pipeline runs zeros through the banks so that the objects catch up with the core, and puts what comes out on the queues without the clip gain that every frame before it was multiplied by. In 22 of the 24 JOC streams of the corpus every payload says a gain of one (`verify --json`, `joc.clipgain_x1000`), and there it is nothing; the other two say 1.031 and 1.063 in some of their frames. It is what the command did before and does now: whether it is right is a question for the decoder it is measured against, and not for a change that moves no byte.

reading: Taking the rows of a delivery of objects off the queues was 11.9 to 13.1 per cent of the command, and writing them 9.5 to 11.1. With the rows in one buffer, the samples of an object straight on its queue and the writers filling buffers that are given their size first, a delivery takes 83.5 to 85.0 per cent of the time it took, on one stream of each kind of JOC stream in the corpus. The object deliveries of TrueHD streams, which go through the same writers, take 97.3 to 99.2 per cent bound to the fast cores. Every delivery of the corpus is the same byte for byte.
